common_name: Flexuosa Alba Nerine (White Wavy-Petaled Guernsey Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: This white-flowered selection from the Flexuosa Group bears small clusters of pure white, wavy-edged flowers on stout stems in late autumn, after the species' more common pink form has usually finished blooming. Narrow, strap-shaped leaves emerge alongside or just after the flowers and persist through winter before dying back the following season. It has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its dependable performance in sheltered, sunny borders with sharp drainage. In the coldest parts of its range a deep, dry mulch over winter, or growing it in a container that can be moved under cover, helps it survive.

common_name: Quinton Wells Nerine (Crimped Pink Hardy Guernsey Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun.

directions: Quinton Wells produces bright pink flowers with distinctively crimped, narrow petals held in full umbels that open slightly earlier than most other bowdenii selections, typically from August into October. Its broad, strap-shaped leaves can grow noticeably longer than those of many hardy nerine cultivars, giving the clump a lusher look once flowering finishes. The cultivar traces back to bulbs collected in the northern Drakensberg by Dr. Arthur Quinton Wells and introduced into English gardens in the late 1940s, and it has since received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It tolerates drier, shadier spots better than many other bowdenii cultivars, though full sun in lean, sharply drained soil still produces the heaviest bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs shallowly in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this winter-growing, summer-dormant Cape species should be kept completely dry once its leaves die down in late spring.

directions: Eucomis regia is the type species of the pineapple lily genus and the only one that grows and flowers through the cool, wet Cape winter rather than in summer. Low rosettes of flat, ground-hugging leaves surround a short, stout flower stalk bearing green, faintly unpleasant-scented blossoms in late winter and early spring, topped by an oversized tuft of leafy bracts. Because its growth cycle runs opposite to nearly every other garden bulb, it is best grown in a container where watering can be timed to its winter-active, summer-dormant habit rather than in an open border watered on a typical summer schedule. Its diminutive size suits rock gardens, troughs, and bulb frames.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant large bulbs 6-8 inches deep in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this subspecies produces the largest bulbs and tallest flower spikes in the genus and may take a season or two to reach full size.

directions: The largest of all pineapple lilies, this subspecies of Eucomis pallidiflora sends up flower spikes that can reach six feet, densely packed with pale yellow-green, star-shaped flowers below the genus's signature pineapple-like tuft of leafy bracts. Broad, wavy-margined leaves can stretch two feet long, giving the whole plant an outsized, almost tropical presence despite being a fully temperate South African native. In the wild it grows in seasonally wet vleis and marshy grassland, so it appreciates more consistent moisture through the growing season than most other eucomis. Its sheer scale makes it a dramatic architectural specimen at the back of a border or beside a pond.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; this Cape Peninsula endemic roots in over the cool winter months and sends up its tall flower spikes the following early summer.

directions: Table Mountain watsonia produces some of the tallest flower spikes in the genus, with twenty to thirty large, flared, tubular blooms ranging from deep reddish orange to salmon-pink arranged in neat rows along stems that can top four feet. Long, sword-shaped leaves form substantial basal clumps beneath the flowering stems, which appear in early summer. It is a narrow endemic restricted to the Cape Peninsula, occurring on rocky slopes from Kalk Bay to Table Mountain itself, so plants in cultivation trace back to a fairly limited wild gene pool. Like other Cape watsonias, it grows through the cool, moist winter and appreciates a dry rest after flowering finishes.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
